title: What Travels, What Stays
author: Nadina Lisbon
summary: Nadina Lisbon uses two recent standards developments to ask what stays distinctive about an organization when AI agent plumbing becomes shared. Four competing companies contributed pieces of their agent stacks, including Agent Skills and Open Responses, to a neutral Linux Foundation home, while the IETF started a working group on agent communication protocols. She argues that a skill file is a team's know-how written down, so portable formats make that effort outlast any single vendor. What does not travel is the judgment about whether the work was good, which no standards body can define for a given customer, risk appetite, or sense of craft. She cites a preprint in which fixing a scoring defect dropped an agent benchmark's measured success from 94.3 to 65.5 percent, as a reminder that measuring is harder than plumbing. Her five-minute exercise asks leaders to write a two-sentence definition of good for one agent-assisted workflow and test whether the team's score would catch it.
points: Agent formats are becoming shared infrastructure, so competitive advantage shifts to the judgment about what counts as good work.
A skill file is a team's institutional know-how in written form, and open formats make that know-how portable across vendors.
A single scoring choice can change a benchmark result dramatically, so leaders should keep a person close to how success is defined.
The five-minute exercise has two sentences: what a good outcome looks like in the customer's terms, and one way a run could pass and still disappoint.
The review question to bring to the team is what the reported score would miss.
quotes: What doesn’t travel is the judgment about whether the work was good. A standards body can agree on how a request is shaped or how a sandbox runs.
A skill file is, in a very human sense, a team’s know-how written down. Until recently, most of that writing lived wherever one vendor’s tool happened to keep it.

Every agent that works well inside an organization carries a little of that organization’s judgment. Someone sat down and wrote out how a refund should be handled, which system holds the real customer record, what tone works with a nervous client.
When the formats become shared, the judgment about what counts as good work stays with you.

Write one sentence describing what a good outcome looks like to you, in your customer’s terms rather than the system’s. Write a second sentence naming one way a run could be marked “successful” and still disappoint you.
After a scoring defect was corrected across 4,320 episodes, measured success fell from 94.3% to 65.5%
